name: Governance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Who Decides? Blockchain's Missing Org Chart
lesson.summary: Public blockchains have no CEO or board, yet someone still has to decide how the software changes, so governance is the set of processes, formal and informal, that stakeholders use to make and enforce those decisions.
lesson.body:
Building on the blockchain definition from earlier in this book, a blockchain is a shared, append-only ledger maintained by a distributed set of participants without a central operator. That absence of a central operator raises a question traditional software rarely has to answer as urgently: when the rules need to change, who gets to change them? Governance is the umbrella term for the processes, formal and informal, by which a blockchain's stakeholders propose, debate, decide, and implement changes to the protocol's rules, and resolve disputes when the rules themselves are ambiguous or contested.

A useful way into governance is to run the stakeholder analysis this book introduced earlier and ask who actually has power over a given chain, and what each group wants. Core developers write and review the code, but they cannot force anyone to run it. Miners or validators decide, block by block, which version of the software they point their hardware or stake at. Node operators choose whether to install an upgrade at all, and their collective choice actually defines the canonical chain, since a rule only holds if enough nodes enforce it. Token holders may or may not have formal votes depending on the design, but they always have an economic stake in the outcome. Exchanges and custodians decide which chain to list and support after a contested change, which in practice hands them real influence over which fork survives economically. These groups' interests do not automatically align, and governance is what happens when they do not.

In a centralized system, a vendor can simply ship a breaking change and users either accept it or leave. A public blockchain cannot do that cleanly, because part of its value proposition is that the rules will not be changed unilaterally out from under participants. That constraint is a feature, not a bug, but it means every meaningful protocol change has to earn the voluntary cooperation of a dispersed and often anonymous set of stakeholders, none of whom can be compelled.

The starkest illustration of a blockchain governance failure, and recovery, is The DAO hack of 2016. The DAO was a smart contract based investment fund built on Ethereum that raised a large sum of ether from thousands of participants; an attacker exploited a re-entrancy flaw in its code and drained a significant portion of those funds into a child contract. Ethereum had no formal on-chain mechanism to reverse the theft, so the community debated, largely off-chain, whether to execute a hard fork that would effectively undo the hack by moving the stolen funds to a recovery contract. The fork went through, becoming what is now called Ethereum, but a minority of participants who believed the ledger should never be altered, no matter the circumstance, continued running the original, unforked chain, which persists today as Ethereum Classic. That single decision was blockchain governance operating in the most visible way possible: a contested proposal, an informal but real vote by node operators choosing which software to run, and a permanent split when consensus could not be reached.

The rest of this chapter looks at two broad strategies blockchains use to make these decisions less chaotic than The DAO episode: on-chain governance, which encodes voting and execution directly into the protocol, and off-chain governance, which keeps decision-making in human forums and relies on voluntary adoption of the resulting software. Neither fully solves the coordination problem; they just distribute where the friction sits.
